items.summary: Post-training compression of pretrained medical segmentation models commonly uses quantization, pruning, or distillation to reduce model size and computational cost. Existing medical segmentation quantization studies mainly evaluate Dice, model size, memory, and latency, but this is incomplete for safety-critical use because compressed models should also preserve uncertainty signals that indicate unreliable predictions. We study this problem in compressed MRI/CT segmentation and formalize why Dice can remain stable while uncertainty changes. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (SGAV-MP), a post-training compression framework that selects layer precisions under reliability constraints. SGAV-MP ranks quantization actions with a compact benefit-risk score and accepts them only after full-model reliability validation on a calibration set. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, SGAV-MP preserves FP32-level Dice and high uncertainty-map agreement, achieving $3.59\times$--$7.8\times$ compression in 2D and $4.73\times$--$7.82\times$ in 3D. We also report backend-supported TensorRT deployment measurements separately to distinguish runtime execution from reliability-preserving storage compression.
items.title: Reliability-Preserving Compression for Deployable Medical Image Segmentation

items.summary: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.
items.title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning

items.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies for open-ended generation with natural-language criteria as rewards, but these rewards can become ineffective as training progresses. We identify two failure modes. Under non-discriminative rewards, scores collapse to uniformly low or high values due to insufficient exploration or a mismatch between task difficulty and policy capability. Under spurious rewards, higher scores do not correspond to better responses. Both reflect a training configuration whose task sampling, exploration, and evaluation stay fixed as the policy evolves. We introduce HarnessRL, a training-time harness that co-evolves with the policy through three interfaces for task sampling, rollout guidance, and rubric criteria. HarnessRL maintains a training-time memory from which a harness evolver retrieves within-task history and cross-task evidence. Using this evidence, the evolver attributes each reward failure to the interface whose update can address it. It then runs a proposer and just-in-time critic loop in which the critic accepts a candidate update only after measuring its effect on the current frozen policy, returning rejected candidates for revision. We also curate Rubric-Mix-10k, a five-domain training and evaluation suite for open-ended RL across medical, science, writing, role-play, and instruction-following tasks. On Rubric-Mix-10k, HarnessRL outperforms the strongest baselines by 2.8 to 3.1 points across both 4B and 9B model scales and nearly halves the training steps to its best checkpoint. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Tongyi-ConvAI/Qwen-Character/tree/main/HarnessRL.
items.title: HarnessRL: Co-Evolving Policies with a Just-in-Time Training Harness for Open-Ended RL

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are trained through multi-stage pipelines over heterogeneous data sources, yet developers lack a principled way to pinpoint the specific data responsible for an observed behavior. This lack of observability reduces debugging to reactive patching and makes failures prone to recur under distribution shift or subsequent model updates. To address this limitation, we propose DebugLM, a framework that equips LLMs with built-in data provenance, enabling them to explicitly trace the origins of their behaviors to specific training data sources. Specifically, the model learns to associate its responses with unique provenance tags that indicate the responsible dataset, empowering developers to precisely identify where undesirable behaviors are learned. Building on this capability, DebugLM further supports targeted test-time remediation, enabling developers to selectively trigger targeted refusal for specified data sources without retraining or modifying model parameters. Experiments demonstrate that DebugLM provides accurate behavior tracing in multi-stage training pipelines and effective test-time remediation while preserving the general utility of the model.
items.title: DebugLM: Learning Traceable Training Data Provenance for LLMs

items.summary: Modeling-ready feature matrices and machine-readable results of the corrected modeling campaign (v3) reported in the article "Protocol-Induced Optimism and Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Failure in Feature-Based Lithium-Ion Battery RUL Prediction" (Energies, submitted). Seven public lithium-ion aging datasets (CALCE, HUST, MATR, NASA randomized usage, Oxford, NASA PCoE, XJTU), charge and discharge phases, remaining useful life to 80% of the estimated initial capacity (threshold arm at 85%). This version supersedes 1.0.x. The matrices of version 1.0.x contained five capacity-trend descriptors computed over each cell's whole trajectory (temporal leakage) and voltage-capacity curve features for the MATR domain only; results derived from them are not the ones reported in the article. Files: modeling_ready_t80.tar and modeling_ready_t85.tar (feature matrix, target and identifiers per phase at the 80% and 85% thresholds); features_causal.tar (per-dataset feature parquets with history-only trend descriptors and the v3 targets); campanha_v3_results.zip (metrics of all 5,976 fits of the core matrix, the threshold arm, the 20 repeated partitions and the nested source-only selection; permutation importance; learning curves; aggregated tables; integrity gates; logs; per-cell target audit; checksums; frozen environment); supplementary_data_S1-S7.zip (Supplementary Data S1 to S7 of the article as consolidated CSV files, with a column dictionary in the README). SHA256 of every parquet in RELEASE_CHECKSUMS.json and of the three archives in MATRICES_sha256.txt; the companion code record (campanha_v3 1.1.0) verifies them and regenerates the tables. The raw datasets are not redistributed; see the article for sources and licenses. Predictions and model binaries were not saved.
items.title: Protocol-Induced Optimism and Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Failure in Feature-Based Lithium-Ion Battery RUL Prediction: feature matrices and campaign results (v1.1.0, corrected campaign)

items.summary: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
items.title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing

items.summary: Fault localization (FL) aims to identify code locations responsible for software failures and is commonly evaluated by how accurately it ranks known fault locations. Large language model (LLM) agents are changing program repair and are increasingly used to search and reason over repositories. Although recent LLM-based FL methods have improved localization accuracy, their impact on agentic repair remains unclear. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic empirical study of FL in agentic repair. We evaluate six recent FL methods on SWE-bench Verified and Defects4J with three LLMs under a common repair framework and analyze 16,248 repair trajectories. We also examine gold locations and bug-cause descriptions as forms of FL guidance across different repair contexts. The studied FL methods do not consistently improve repair success, and higher localization accuracy does not consistently lead to larger repair gains. Yet FL guides agents' early search and helps them reach relevant code sooner. Accurate locations can reduce repair token use by up to 39.2\%, but current FL methods often consume more tokens than they save during repair. Experiments with gold guidance suggest that FL has greater potential when bug inputs contain fewer location clues. Providing bug causes can further improve repair success beyond locations alone. We also find that ground truth from a single reference patch does not fully capture the locations used by successful repairs. These findings help clarify the value of FL in agentic repair and inform future work on its design and evaluation.
items.title: From Finding to Fixing: How Useful is Fault Localization for Agentic Program Repair?

items.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from pairwise preferences through a logistic objective whose score-difference parameterization follows the Bradley--Terry model. We study how failure of this modeling assumption limits DPO, distinguishing structural misspecification from limited model capacity and finite-sample estimation. Our main contribution is a characterization of structural approximation error through the triangle-curl of the preference log-odds, which vanishes exactly when preferences admit a Bradley--Terry representation. We upper bound the achievable excess logistic risk by a score-class approximation term and a triangle-curl term, and establish a lower bound proportional to triangle-curl under additional boundedness assumptions. For ReLU score models, including clipped models, we derive explicit approximation rates showing that increasing capacity can eliminate the score-approximation term while leaving the structural obstruction unchanged. We further establish finite-sample bounds for clipped empirical risk minimizers that separate network approximation, structural misspecification, and estimation error. We place these results within a surrogate-risk framework by identifying contextual preference accuracy (CPA) as a natural measure of agreement between preference judgments and changes in pairwise probability ratios relative to the reference policy. Standard logistic consistency and calibration results connect DPO's objective to this policy property and transfer our excess-risk upper bounds to CPA, without treating CPA as a complete measure of generated-response quality.
items.title: Statistical Learning Theory for Direct Preference Optimization

items.summary: Code, independent checks and the record of the Anaxia engine for the paper Which String Vibrations Become Which Generations on the Dwork Quintic by Deep Bhattacharjee and Ushashi Bhattacharya. The paper determines, for the heterotic string with the standard embedding on the one-parameter family of quintic threefolds, which vibration modes become which families of charged particles. The 101 families are labelled by 101 distinct characters of the symmetry group (Z/5)^3, and the 24 characters that do not occur are the classes of the permutations of (0,1,2,3,4). Every Yukawa coupling allowed by the symmetry is a power of the modulus, psi^r with r = 0, 1, 2, 3 on 566, 425, 280 and 160 unordered triples, and every other coupling vanishes. The invariant deformation pairs each family with exactly one partner, so that the mass matrix has determinant psi^70, full rank away from the Fermat point and rank 51 there, where the masses are given in closed form by the Gamma function. The Geometric Selection Conjecture is shown to be equivalent to the existence of one viable vacuum fixed by mirror symmetry, and no smooth quintic and no free quotient of one carries three families. The existence of a viable vacuum is open. The archive holds 64 independent checks: a C program for the labels, the couplings allowed by the group and the mass map, a C++ expansion of the Hessian over its 120 permutations, Python checks of the socle, the Hessian, the intersection form of the Fermat quintic and the Gamma values, a Julia check of the Hodge norms, a Macaulay2 computation of the Jacobian ring at two rational values of the modulus with the socle functional on all 3876 monomials of degree fifteen, and 11 Lean 4 theorems on the counts and the arithmetic of the Hessian, each axiom-free or depending on propext only. code/run_checks.sh runs them all. code/bllm/ holds the failure, change and retry record of the four targets on the Anaxia engine (release 3.0.5, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23469389).
items.title: Which String Vibrations Become Which Generations on the Dwork Quintic: code, checks and engine record

items.summary: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.
items.title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents

items.summary: A small justification for a rule-based conclusion may disappear when a source is withdrawn, and multiple derivations need not provide independent evidence. We study minimum-cost certificates that preserve a Horn conclusion under every withdrawal of at most k source domains. Evidence records remain distinct from asserted facts, supporting replicated attestations and overlapping failure dependencies. Transversals of minimal-support footprints characterize robustness and explain why disjoint-proof requirements can reject valid certificates. An exact procedure alternates weighted evidence selection with a source-failure oracle. A rule-closed counterinterpretation yields a globally valid selection cut without enumerating supports or failure scenarios. We prove correctness, finite termination, and cost optimality, establish coNP-completeness of unrestricted verification and NP-completeness of synthesis for every fixed budget, and identify a tractable reachability restriction. Experiments on controlled benchmarks, reachability graphs, and ontology-derived instances demonstrate that our counterinterpretation-guided synthesis achieves up to 92% optimum coverage within practical resource bounds, outperforming scenario expansion and general abduction while confirming the necessity of transversal-based reasoning over proof-packing heuristics.
items.title: Minimum-Cost Robust Evidence Certificates for Horn Reasoning under Correlated Source Failures

items.summary: 🌟 Summary Ultralytics 8.4.183 expands hardware deployment and improves reliability across training, prediction, data handling, and evaluation. 🚀 📊 Key Changes Axelera Metis support for every YOLO26 task: With Voyager SDK 1.9.0, detection, instance and semantic segmentation, depth estimation, pose, OBB, and classification models can all export, predict, and validate through yolo . The NMS-free detection path is used by default. SDK 1.8 exports remain compatible; the updated setup requires metis-dkms 1.7.0 or newer and supports PyTorch versions below 2.15. Higher Axelera throughput: In the documented COCO128 benchmark, SDK 1.9 reached 109 images per second at batch 32 , compared with 40 images per second on SDK 1.8. Larger prediction batches can improve throughput; batch size 1 remains useful when per-image latency matters. Intel acceleration for LiteRT models: LiteRT exports can now run on Intel CPUs and NPUs, including support for YOLO26 task types such as detection, segmentation, depth, pose, OBB, and classification. More reliable training and depth calibration: Fixes address warmup and gradient accumulation edge cases, MPS memory growth during training, and depth calibration replacing an already-good calibration with a worse one. Interrupted runs can also resume under the same Ultralytics Platform model, and W&B resuming works on Windows. More accurate and robust data workflows: Fixes improve ImageNet-subset classifier validation, accept UTF-8 labels with a byte-order mark, preserve non-ASCII grounding annotations, convert COCO RLE masks for segmentation, and align 16-bit NumPy images with image-file prediction behavior. Prediction, export, and visualization fixes: Negative FastSAM points now reliably exclude masks regardless of prompt order. Other fixes cover very thin images, rectangular INT8 calibration, grayscale LiteRT models, semantic overlay colors, depth-map saving, and several additional edge cases. Platform and documentation updates: Platform documentation now includes Gemma 4 and Nemotron as hosted annotation models and explains new visibility controls and workflows. Benchmark instructions were also clarified for NMS-free evaluation. 🎯 Purpose & Impact Deploy YOLO26 on more hardware and tasks: Axelera users can use one integrated workflow across all seven YOLO26 tasks, while Intel LiteRT users gain CPU and NPU inference options. Get better throughput when processing batches: Axelera SDK 1.9 can substantially increase prediction throughput for larger batches, though actual results depend on hardware and workload. Trust training, validation, and predictions more: The fixes reduce avoidable failures and make reported results better reflect the supplied data and model—for example, correcting classifier label alignment changes ImageNette validation accuracy from 9.45% to 70.37% in the reported test. Keep existing workflows working: Many changes are targeted bug fixes or compatibility improvements; notably, Axelera models exported with SDK 1.8 do not need to be re-exported for SDK 1.9. What's Changed Fix R/B channel swap of semantic mask overlays in train/val mosaics by @cainiao33 in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/26755 Scale 16-bit NumPy prediction inputs to 8 bits by @Nikhi00718 in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/26741 Restore pre-existing temporary module aliases by @Vaishnavi220506 in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/26756 Respect negative FastSAM points regardless of prompt order by @Nikhi00718 in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/26759 Align ImageNet subset folders with classifier class IDs by @Nikhi00718 in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/26760 Fix INT8 calibration crash when exporting with rect=True by @Y-T-G in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/26750 Fix LiteRT layout detection for grayscale exports by @aswanth-07 in https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/26747 Clamp warmup accumulate ramp to the capped
items.title: Ultralytics YOLO

items.summary: Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback for policy learning and execution monitoring. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Our results reveal errors in fine-grained instruction grounding, history-dependent progress tracking, and recovery assessment, even in models with strong outcome and forward-progress scores. The same semantic subtask can also receive substantially different value gains across valid execution orders. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. The website is available at https://robovalue-benchmark.github.io/.
items.title: RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models

items.summary: Distributed LLM serving relies on a global index to locate reusable key-value cache (KVCache) blocks through prefix matching. Losing the index after a crash or restart forces affected requests to recompute existing KVCache on GPUs. Persisting the index restores access after a failure. Existing persistent indexes face a tension between prefix-matching performance and recovery time. A snapshot-backed in-memory index supports fast prefix matching, but rebuilding the full index delays recovery. An on-SSD index avoids this rebuild, but adds storage accesses to prefix matching. Our core insight is that extending a matched prefix over a short span typically requires distinguishing only a few token sequences, suggesting that sparse in-memory routing state may suffice. Prefix matching also accesses block metadata in sequence order, allowing metadata for consecutive blocks to be retrieved together. We present SARP (Sparse Adaptive Routing and Packing), an on-SSD KVCache index for fast recovery and prefix matching. SARP groups consecutive block IDs and metadata into segments to amortize storage accesses across multiple blocks. A compact in-memory routing directory identifies candidate segments using entries at selected block positions. SARP limits segment retrievals and uses compact filters to prioritize candidates with longer potential matches. After retrieval, SARP verifies block IDs against the query and reuses only KVCache blocks covered by the verified prefix. After a restart, SARP restores the sparse routing directory from a snapshot. Across four multi-turn chat and agentic workloads, SARP recovers 8.0x to 77.5x faster than the in-memory index baselines and delivers 1.15x to 66.6x the request throughput of the on-SSD index baselines, while reusing only 0.0030% to 0.029% fewer tokens than exact prefix matching.
items.title: SARP: An On-SSD Index for KVCache with Fast Prefix Matching and Recovery

items.summary: Code, independent checks and the record of the Anaxia engine for the paper Which String Vibrations Become Which Generations on the Dwork Quintic by Deep Bhattacharjee and Ushashi Bhattacharya. The paper determines, for the heterotic string with the standard embedding on the one-parameter family of quintic threefolds, which vibration modes become which families of charged particles. The 101 families are labelled by 101 distinct characters of the symmetry group (Z/5)^3, and the 24 characters that do not occur are the classes of the permutations of (0,1,2,3,4). Every Yukawa coupling allowed by the symmetry is a power of the modulus, psi^r with r = 0, 1, 2, 3 on 566, 425, 280 and 160 unordered triples, and every other coupling vanishes. The invariant deformation pairs each family with exactly one partner, so that the mass matrix has determinant psi^70, full rank away from the Fermat point and rank 51 there, where the masses are given in closed form by the Gamma function. The Geometric Selection Conjecture is shown to be equivalent to the existence of one viable vacuum fixed by mirror symmetry, and no smooth quintic and no free quotient of one carries three families. On the three other one-parameter pencils of Fermat type, the sextic in P(1,1,1,1,2), the octic in P(1,1,1,1,4) and the dectic in P(1,1,1,2,5), the 103, 149 and 145 families carry only 96, 122 and 100 distinct characters of symmetry groups of order 108, 128 and 100; every coupling allowed by the symmetry is psi^r times a product of weights; the mass map of the invariant direction has rank 99, 125 and 109 at every member with psi nonzero, so 4, 24 and 36 families stay massless; and no member or free quotient carries three families. The existence of a viable vacuum is open. The archive holds 121 independent checks: a C program for the labels, the couplings allowed by the group and the mass map, a C++ expansion of the Hessian over its 120 permutations, Python checks of the socle, the Hessian, the intersection form of the Fermat quintic and the Gamma values, a Julia check of the Hodge norms, a Macaulay2 computation of the Jacobian ring at two rational values of the modulus with the socle functional on all 3876 monomials of degree fifteen, Python and Macaulay2 checks of the labels, characters, couplings, Jacobian rings and mass maps of the three weighted pencils, and 14 Lean 4 theorems on the counts, the arithmetic of the Hessian and the numbers of the weighted pencils, each axiom-free or depending on propext only. code/run_checks.sh runs them all. code/bllm/ holds the failure, change and retry record of the five targets on the Anaxia engine (release 3.1.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23484160).

items.summary: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.
items.title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts

items.summary: Version 2.3 of Adversarial Multi-AI Falsification is a bounded case study of AI-assisted scholarly workflow governance. It distinguishes selected public verbatim excerpts and message/line maps from author-reported recovery findings and hashes identifying internal artifacts. The public deposit does not contain the full captured transcripts or executed rubric. Four process-failure types required exclusion or downgrading: semantic drift with unsupported process certification; assignment-scope expansion; prior-task substitution; and unverified or misdescribed legal citations. E2 remains partial. The principal execution/adjudication sequence remains author-reconstructed, and panel unanimity cannot be independently recomputed from the public deposit. The operational proposition remains untested; this revision does not establish it as true. The paper proposes a three-field outcome record and six workflow controls, including a two-turn assignment-echo checkpoint. These are unvalidated design propositions, not demonstrated interventions. This is a case report and protocol demonstration, not a benchmark, product comparison, prevalence estimate or complete reproducibility study. AMAF_v2_3.pdf is the current controlling manuscript, with AMAF_v2_3.docx as its editable counterpart. All seven v2.2 files are retained unchanged as historical records, including the old preparation-candidate manuscript, README, manifest and checksum list. Read 00_README_AMAF_v2_3_RELEASE.txt for the current controlling-version guide; AMAF_v2_3_SHA256SUMS.txt lists this release's file identities. The historical v1.8 paper is retained only for its Section C dual-track summary. No additional private records, new experiment or new empirical validation are released. Generative AI systems were used for structured literature discovery, comparative issue mapping, adversarial review, source-check planning, language editing and revision support. They are not authors. The human author retains responsibility for the sources, interpretations, arguments and conclusions.
items.title: Adversarial Multi-AI Falsification in Research Workflows: A Bounded Case Study of Scope Error, Verification Failure, and Human Adjudication

items.summary: RECONFIGURABLE ROBOTIC SWARMS AND CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONAL REGENERATION AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | White Rainbow Scientific Library | Flagship 02 Prospective Research Atlas — English Review Edition, October 2026 Can a distributed population of heterogeneous modular robots reconstruct an operationally qualified capability after damage, without treating a newly assembled shape as evidence of restored function? Reconfigurable Robotic Swarms and Continuous Functional Regeneration at the Limit develops an interdisciplinary research program on modular morphology, distributed self-assembly, task-dependent graph structure, mechanical qualification, connector fatigue, recoverable actions, and independent post-reconfiguration verification. Its central proposition is deliberately testable: a swarm may change its topology after losing modules, but it earns the stronger name of functional regeneration only when its restored configuration satisfies the original, independently assessed service requirements and does not conceal emerging hazards or latent joint failures. The monograph distinguishes three often conflated networks: mechanical connections that transmit forces, communication links that transmit information, and power connections that transport energy. It then investigates how graph connectivity, geometric rigidity, elastic stiffness, buckling, frictional contact, thermal dissipation, material fatigue, sensing uncertainty, local negotiation, and safe rollback constrain what an apparently repaired swarm can actually do. A prospective twenty-module testbed provides recurring engineering anchors: bridge, gripping, and sensing-tower tasks, blinded removal of modules, unseen configurations, independent qualification, and strong comparisons with redundant fixed structures and specialist replacement procedures. The research architecture includes thirty mathematically diverse derivation plates, eighty-two chapter-level questions and their five individually paginated study units, two hundred falsifiable Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. The companion spreadsheet links physical models, chapter topics, prospective study cards, provenance, source DOI records, and page references to support future research and AI-assisted scientific handoff. Published robotics literature supplies a source-grounded context for modular reconfigurable mechanisms and fault-aware planning, including external DOI records for reviews and an existing fault-tolerant modular system. The manuscript separates those precedents from its own unexecuted research designs. Its two STARLI mother volumes are listed as conceptual ancestry, not as independent experimental validation. Biological regeneration functions as an analogy for staged assessment of restoration, not as evidence of biomedical efficacy, autonomous human-tissue repair, or indefinite machine life. This is a prospective research-atlas REVIEW EDITION. The mathematical relations, study proposals, design seeds, and acceptance thresholds are not experimentally validated findings. External mathematical review, whole-text DOI auditing, and a stronger editorial review for chapter-level semantic repetition remain necessary before scholarly publication. Negative findings, conventional method superiority, irreversible module retirement, and scientific abstention are legitimate outcomes within this research program. STARLI | 33 | White Rainbow Scientific Library

items.summary: Source code of the article "Protocol-Induced Optimism and Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Failure in Feature-Based Lithium-Ion Battery RUL Prediction" (Energies, submitted). Version 1.1.0 keeps the feature-extraction pipeline of version 1.0.x and adds campanha_v3-1.1.0.zip, the package that produced every result reported in the article. campanha_v3 is an auditable re-run of the modeling campaign: the v1.0.x modeling sources exactly as they ran (pristine/, SHA256), one script per correction with its unified diff (patches/), the patched sources (patched/), new modules for target re-join with history-only trend descriptors, causality and coverage gates, preflight, nested source-only selection, aggregation and release verification (new/), synthetic-data tests with a CI workflow (tests/), the ordered pipeline with gates (scripts/), and docs/ with the change log (file and line references), the SHA256 of the archived feature matrices and result tables (RELEASE_CHECKSUMS.json) and the frozen HPC environment (pip_freeze.txt; Python 3.13, scikit-learn 1.9.0). Defects removed relative to 1.0.x: whole-trajectory capacity-trend descriptors used as features (temporal leakage), deny-list feature selection, per-cell curve validity flags in the matrix, unaudited right-censoring, hard-coded end-of-life threshold and permanence, duplicate feature configurations, untruncated negative predictions, shared seed for partition and estimators, fixed ElasticNet, and a source-only selection that used target-trained models. Details in docs/CHANGELOG.md. The feature matrices and the results are in the companion data record. "bash scripts/verify_release.sh" recomputes the checksums, counts the fits (2,520 core, 360 threshold arm, 1,920 repeated partitions, 1,176 nested selection) and regenerates the manuscript tables from the archived metrics.
items.title: Battery RUL Prediction Framework: Reproducible Machine Learning Pipeline

items.summary: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.
items.title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data

items.summary: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.
items.title: StebBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents

items.summary: Assembly traces can support explicit probabilistic inference without being treated as recovered program meaning. Active Assembly Theory and Practice makes that distinction executable: transparent x86-64 fixtures are decoded with Capstone, traced under bounded Unicorn emulation, and mapped to typed observations that distinguish missing, unseen, and unsupported evidence. Two Generalized Notation Notation (GNN) specifications define passive-phase and prospective sensor models whose tensors drive real pymdp execution. A native categorical Julia/RxInfer companion consumes the passive model's same parameters (Friedman 2026; Heins et al. 2022; Bagaev et al. 2023). The sensor Agent selects an action before fixture evidence is acquired. Independent finite calculations check beliefs and policy scores; native smoothing uses the same parameters and first-observation convention. Every inference comparator and fitted diagnostic also consumes an upstream-parsed numeric GNN specification, with source-bound runtime instances and rendered model graphs. A corpus of 10 authored fixtures supports complete-fixture exclusion diagnostics. At the fixed informative likelihood, the memoryless decoder outperforms the temporal filter; temporal advantages appear under synthetic observation ambiguity. Designed category ambiguity remains a visible failure case. The separate Gaussian and categorical Bethe free-energy diagnostics are not compared numerically with policy expected free energy. The quotient benchmark contains 64 transformation-family identifiers and 4096 rows, with 16 families held out from model fitting. The co-primary portfolio includes an interpretable classifier, a temporal probabilistic model, a fixed one-layer tanh recurrent classifier, and surface baselines; the temporal endpoint reaches balanced accuracy 0.775 and macro-F1 0.772 on this frozen bounded benchmark. Held-out identifiers share authored template lineages with the fitting data. Family-resampling intervals and conditional randomization diagnostics therefore describe this finite inventory; the retrospective protocol correction withholds superiority claims. A complementary pinned static-only corpus supplies 5 licensed source projects and 100 source-contract rows, including 40 lexical witnesses, 40 contract-directed near misses, and 20 identity controls. The corpus establishes provenance and coverage; it does not execute arbitrary external binaries or support application-effectiveness claims. Selected normalized machine-state relations are checked by Python, native execution, and a bounded Lean fragment. Exact finite sensing certificates and source-bound reader artifacts make assumptions and failures inspectable. Independent physical replication remains unearned. The contribution is a reproducible substrate for testing assembly-to-inference mechanisms, with explicit limits on semantics, statistical generalization, and external validity.
items.title: Active Assembly Theory and Practice

( #2833 , #2834 , #2864 ) Dropped jurors whose judges returned no parsable score and excluded unparsable scores from per-item averages. ( #2837 , #2917 ) Excluded unparsable scores from BatchEvaluator aggregation, leaderboard averages, and compare_runs . ( #2866 , #2905 , #2939 ) Guardrails now reject unparsable and non-finite scores. ( #2902 ) Validated structured-output scores against the configured scale and corrected chain-of-thought context relevance scoring to use the requested scale. ( #2836 , #2860 ) Added response labeling to the agreement judge prompt. ( #2835 ) Added validation for retrieval relevance score lengths. ( #2853 ) Deduplicated ideal DCG by golden chunk text in ndcg_at_k . ( #2857 ) Skipped non-finite predictions during few-shot selection. ( #2852 ) Preserved min_score_val , max_score_val , and temperature in Metric.with_arguments . ( #2922 ) Fixed a pandas 3 get_group error when there is a single evaluation root. ( #2937 ) Corrected the llm_provider module import in jury.py . ( #2869 ) Batch evaluation and core behavior Read batch column mappings from the original row and preserved results when output column names collide. ( #2845 , #2844 ) Kept BatchEvaluator independent of the optional feedback package. ( #2901 ) Treated missing DataFrame cells as None and preserved columns in empty batch DataFrames. ( #2942 , #2946 ) Preserved retrieval order in context_filter results. ( #2932 ) Added a warning when TruSession is re-created with different settings. ( #2944 ) Cost accounting and reporting Prevented nested cost scopes from leaking callbacks into their parent scope. ( #2872 ) Fixed double-counting of evaluation spend in eval_cost . ( #2855 ) Google provider cost accounting now includes thinking tokens and can price responses without constructing a client.
