items.title: truera/trulens: TruLens 2.16.0

items.summary: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.
items.title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models

items.summary: Supporting data and analysis code for the manuscript submitted to Digital Discovery (RSC). The paper traces a cobalt-specific failure of conditional crystal generation back to one row of the public training data. Every number reported in the manuscript is recomputed from the files in this deposit by a single script (`verify_all_numbers.py`), which prints a mismatch count. This deposit is self-contained except for the training archive itself, which is 186 MB and is redistributed by its original authors; its exact provenance and checksum are recorded in `alex_mp_20_snapshot.json` so that the identical snapshot can be retrieved. Version v4 (revision). Adds the canonical generated structure files (5,121 chemical systems, 40,968 CIFs, assigned by reproducing the audit table system by system), the structures of the pre-registered generation tests, the generation command template and job files, the revision analyses (pre-registered tests A and B, equivalence test, upstream comparisons of the Co–O entries and hull vertices, DFT runs D1–D4) with the revision pre-registration, the figure-library modules and the recorded package versions. Element-level results are recomputed on the canonical set; the hull, DFT and intervention results of v1–v3 are unchanged. The verifier runs inside the deposit with relative paths and reports 0 mismatches.
items.title: Data and code for: A single reference-energy outlier nearly eliminates Co–O chemistry from a generative model's training distribution

items.summary: Open radio access network (O-RAN) enables a multi-vendor ecosystem that accelerates xApp development for near-real-time (RT) network management. However, this openness shifts a combinatorial coordination burden to the Non-RT layer, where rApp policies compose xApps from a growing catalog to realize operator intents. Coexisting intents further compound this challenge, as conflicts may arise among xApp actions, rApp policies, and their cross-layer interactions. To maximize intent admission while maintaining key performance indicator (KPI) compliance across incoming and incumbent intents, we propose a large language model-based Multi-Agentic AI framework. A Reasoning Agent screens candidate xApps against KPI contracts and produces a joint intent admission and xApp assignment decision. On post-deployment KPI violations, a Diagnosis Agent identifies the root causes of failure, labels the conflict mechanism, and guides the Reasoning Agent in subsequent attempts. Experimental results show that the framework based on GPT-OSS 120B achieves 28.6% more KPI-compliant cases and admits over 15* as many incoming intents as state-of-the-art baselines. Under the Qwen 72B variant, Diagnosis increases compliant cases by 50.0%, quadruples admitted intents, and reduces deployment attempts by 32.6%. A live deployment conforming to O-RAN specifications further validates the feasibility of the proposed solution for conflict-aware rApp policy orchestration in real networks.
items.title: Multi-Agentic AI for Intent-Driven and Conflict-Aware rApp Policy Orchestration in Open RAN

items.summary: Modeling cascading failure across interdependent critical infrastructure requires either a composable physical simulator per domain or a topological abstraction that discards quantity awareness. Simulators are costly, data-hungry, and require detailed calibration per domain; topological abstractions stay data-parsimonious while missing quantity-based behaviors that govern real dynamics. We present, instead, a knowledge-driven propagation architecture in which heterogeneous service dependencies are identified by categories: a general logical propagation resolves multi-dependency and redundancy structures purely from how nodes are categorized, while quantity-aware categories plug in dedicated mechanisms - here, a max-min fair-share flow module for water distribution. Both share one discrete functionality scale and a monotonic update algorithm guaranteeing convergence in finitely many rounds. We assess the flow module by comparing its results with those we get from preexisting pressure-driven simulation with WNTR (Water Network Tool for Resilience) on eight realistic networks across four failure families (clustered damage, capacity-targeted attack, source failure, tank loss). Under capacity-targeted attack and source failure a topological-reachability baseline misses 46% of the truly critical junctions, where the flow module misses 10% and 8% at an average critical-class precision of 0.73. Supplementary materials, code and results are available at: https://github.com/cascade-platform-org/CASCADE
items.title: Composable, Knowledge-Driven Disservice Propagation for Complex Interdependent Services with a Flow-Allocation Module Validated Against Hydraulic Simulation

items.summary: Serverless computing is increasingly used to run complex DAG workflows across diverse applications, and individual function execution times have grown to support them, pushing workflow makespans to hours. Open-source serverless platforms, deployed on a pool of VMs, typically use on-demand instances, and their cost increases with the makespan. Spot instances are far cheaper, but a preemption is likely before the workflow finishes. A preemption at a fan-out node or a task feeding a fan-in node stalls every parallel branch, cascading a single preemption into a workflow-wide failure. Prior systems address this challenge by migrating high-impact tasks to reliable, non-spot resources, sacrificing spot's cost advantage. We present FaaSpot, a serverless workflow execution system that runs every workflow task on spot instances with no on-demand fallback. Our key insight is that cascade-prone positions are determined by the DAG's topology and can be identified before execution. Therefore, FaaSpot analyzes the workflow DAG once at submission time and classifies each task by the impact of its preemption. Selective checkpointing, survival-aware scaling, and lineage-based retry then act on this single classification, with no runtime coordination. We evaluate FaaSpot on a trace-driven spot emulator with eight DAG workflows against four state-of-the-art baselines. FaaSpot completes 89.03% of runs at $0.018 per successful run, 21pp (percentage points) above the average baseline success rate and at a lower cost per success than every baseline, while reducing mean latency by 2.3x.
items.title: FaaSpot: Fault-Tolerant Serverless Workflow Execution on Spot Instances

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate Verus contracts for Rust programs together with the proofs that establish them. Yet verifier acceptance, the common measure of success, shows only that the implementation satisfies the generated contract, so it leaves open whether the contract captures the intended behavior. Assessing specification generation therefore requires an evaluation methodology, not a single metric. We present VerusEval, a framework that evaluates generated contracts along six dimensions, including Verus-native checks for semantic triviality, validated input-output (I/O) suites, and contract equivalence, and that relates them so that the strength and blind spots of each become measurable. Evaluating 13,716 artifacts from four workflows, five LLMs, and two prompting settings on 762 tasks, we find that acceptance overstates quality: only 42.3\% of the accepted artifacts complete all three semantic checks without a flag, and across workflows and models, higher acceptance does not consistently come with more correct contracts. I/O evaluation rejects 23.6\% of the accepted artifacts, yet only 63.2\% of those that pass it are proved equivalent. Of the accepted artifacts flagged by contract comparison, 84.1\% have a rejected completeness obligation, and the direction of a failure prioritizes inspection of the generated contract or the reference; it does not by itself establish which artifact is defective. Screening and review further identify 36 candidate defects among 61 selected reference contracts, and repairing one of them makes 10 of its 11 failing artifacts equivalent. Based on these findings, we derive four actionable lessons for evaluation, generation, and benchmark maintenance.
items.title: VerusEval: Evaluating LLM-Generated Verus Specifications Beyond Verifier Acceptance

items.summary: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.
items.title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos

items.summary: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.
items.title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence

items.summary: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
items.title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

items.summary: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.
items.title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts

items.summary: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.
items.title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents

items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Of the six benchmarks only the seed conjecture is passed; the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdős problem 1183 stay open. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

items.summary: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.
items.title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise

items.summary: How much classical information can a noisy optical channel carry when both signal energy and preshared entanglement are limited? This work gives an exact capacity frontier for this joint resource problem. It allows one to determine the best asymptotic communication rate, price the benefit of additional entanglement, and distinguish the effect of tolerating errors from that of changing how entanglement is supplied. Exact capacity under two resource constraints The setting is any fixed bosonic Gaussian channel \(\Phi\) with finitely many input and output modes. Signal energy is measured by a positive quadratic Hamiltonian \(H_G=\tfrac12 R^{\mathsf T}GR\), with \(G>0\) and ground energy \(E_0\); \(R\) collects the canonical quadratures. The budgets satisfy \(E\ge E_0\) and \(P\ge0\). For an \(n\)-use code, the mean total signal energy is at most \(nE\), while the same initially shared maximally entangled state has Schmidt rank \(K_n\) satisfying \(\log K_n\le nP\). Thus \(P\) is a strictly supplied entanglement rate. Encoders may be arbitrary joint quantum operations, and decoding may be collective. The classical capacity is \[ C(E,P)=\max_{\substack{U\ge V\;\mathrm{physical}\\ \frac12\operatorname{Tr}(GU)\le E,\;S_G(V)\le P}}\bigl[S_G(\Phi U)+S_G(V)-S_G(\Phi^c V)\bigr]. \] Here \(V\) is a Gaussian seed covariance, \(U\) is the average-input covariance, and \(U-V\) is the displacement-modulation covariance. A covariance is physical when \(V+i\Omega/2\ge0\), where \(\Omega\) is the canonical commutation matrix and the vacuum covariance is \(I/2\). The notation \(S_G\) denotes Gaussian von Neumann entropy, and \(\Phi^c\) is the full complementary channel, including any environment purification. All logarithms are natural, so rates are in nats per channel use. This formula replaces optimization over arbitrary quantum block codes by a finite-dimensional covariance optimization. It supplies both an achievable rate and a converse against non-Gaussian, correlated encodings. At \(P=0\), it also determines the unassisted capacity of general fixed finite-mode Gaussian channels, including channels without a passive decomposition into independent modes. The reduction specifies the exact capacity value; it does not require a closed-form optimizer for every device. Energy and strict entanglement supply respond differently to errors For a fixed allowed average error \(0\le\varepsilon<1\), the exact capacity under the mean-energy constraint is \[ C_\varepsilon(E,P)=C\!\left(E_0+\frac{E-E_0}{1-\varepsilon},\,P\right). \] Allowing failure rescales the mean energy above the ground state, but leaves the strict initial entanglement budget unchanged. The proof uses an exponential strong converse for codes whose inputs obey a hard total-energy cutoff. In a different model, where a readable flag permits random entanglement supply constrained only on average, the work establishes an achievable bound and a strict small-supply advantage for thermal attenuation at positive energy and fixed nonzero error. That comparison identifies the operational importance of the supply rule; it is not a complete capacity characterization of the flagged model. The communication value of entanglement For a thermal attenuator, let \(0<\eta<1\) be the transmissivity, \(b>0\) the output mean photon number for vacuum input, and \(N\) the input mean photon number. Write its capacity as \(C_N(P)\), and define \(g(N)=(N+1)\log(N+1)-N\log N\). The gain from entanglement obeys the sharp bound \[ 0\le C_N(P)-C_N(0)\le\frac{\eta}{1+b}\,P. \] For every fixed \(N>0\), the coefficient \(\eta/(1+b)\) is attained as the initial right derivative at \(P=0\). In the low-photon limit, the stronger resource law is \[ C_N(P)-C_N(0)=\frac{\eta}{1+b}\min\{P,g(N)\}+O(N),\qquad N\downarrow0. \] The remainder is uniform over \(P\ge0\) at fixed \(\eta\) and positive \(b\). Noise therefore determines the conversion efficiency, while \(g(N)\sim N\log(1/N)\) sets the entanglement scale
items.title: A universal energy–entanglement capacity frontier for Gaussian optical channels

items.summary: The macroscopic capabilities of intelligent systems arise from the local interactions of many simple units. When such systems are deployed in the real world, their behaviour must nevertheless be constrained, leaving designers caught between releasing adaptability and preventing loss of control, yet without formal tools to resolve the dilemma. This paper proposes a unified research program for controlled emergence that restates this tension as a pair of dual problems: the forward problem explains macroscopic behaviour from local rules, and the inverse problem solves for controllable rules and readout mechanisms from a desired target. We take an augmented quintuple as the formal object shared by both ends, and decompose ``engineering'' into three independently measurable coordinates: controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability. On this basis we give three testable working hypotheses (critical scale; the cooperation and trade-off between constraint and adaptability; minimal constraint) and one feasibility criterion, which reduce inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking. The program takes explicit failure boundaries as its premise, does not pursue complete control, and always preserves the system's room for self-organization. The reduced pilot experiment attached to this paper serves only to verify the executability of the research protocol and does not constitute a statistical test of the working hypotheses. This design language generalizes to multi-agent artificial intelligence, the industrial internet, and emergency response systems, all of which must confront emergence and controllability at once.
items.title: The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering

items.summary: We investigate quantum-state texture during the thermal relaxation of an anisotropic spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg dimer subject to a longitudinal magnetic field and a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction. Starting from local transverse and longitudinal couplings to a bosonic bath, we construct a global weak-coupling Lindblad equation, identify its transition channels, and discuss the applicability and limitations of the secular approximation. The Gibbs state is obtained explicitly in the local spin basis, revealing that the DM coupling controls both the modulus and phase of the single-excitation coherence by modifying the energy splitting and rotating the chiral phase. For heating and cooling protocols, we compare rugosity, fidelity-based texture, and trace-distance texture with coherence, vector spin chirality, and purity. The relaxation dynamics separates population thermalization from the decay and precession of deliberately prepared energy-basis coherence. Their combined contribution to local coherence produces DM-dependent texture overshoots and, during cooling, damped oscillations and sign changes of the coherence quadratures. These transients differ from the evolution of coherence magnitude and purity, while trace-distance texture weights them differently from the overlap-based quantifiers. Calculations at reduced dissipation preserve the texture maxima within the secular model. The results identify a phase-sensitive diagnostic of relaxation.
items.title: Phase-sensitive quantum-state texture during thermalization of a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Heisenberg dimer

items.summary: AI agents deployed inside organizations can pose an insider threat if they make mistakes, are compromised by an attacker, or pursue misaligned objectives. We propose honeypots as an AI control method to improve the security of internal agent deployments. Rather than only using honeypots for pre-deployment evaluations, defenders should plant decoy opportunities for harmful actions throughout the production environment to detect misbehavior, incriminate malicious agents, and deter attacks. Such honeypots can elicit misbehavior under real deployment conditions, identify malicious agents even if chain-of-thought monitorability degrades, provide reliable warnings about agent misbehavior to security teams, and scale cheaply to many agent instances. The presence of honeypots also introduces uncertainty about which opportunities are real, thus deterring malicious agents from attacking and reducing the rate of misbehavior. We discuss the limitations of honeypots and give reasons to expect them to remain effective as agent capabilities increase. Finally, we outline key research questions to measure and improve the effectiveness of honeypots: testing the robustness of honeypots, comparing their detection effectiveness with other monitoring methods, understanding their incrimination and deterrence effects, and building supporting infrastructure.
items.title: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats

items.summary: This dataset provides monthly global ocean mixed layer depth (MLD) estimates at 1° spatial resolution from January 1982 to December 2023, developed using SJTU-ViT, a Vision Transformer-based reconstruction model. It contains 504 monthly fields on a regular latitude–longitude grid, with valid coverage defined by a fixed RECCAP2 open-ocean mask. The target MLD is defined by a potential density increase of 0.03 kg m⁻³ relative to 10 m. MLD estimates are expressed in metres, positive downward from the sea surface, with a lower bound of 10 m. Data are provided in NetCDF-4 format, accompanied by a README describing the variables, coordinates, MLD definition, masking, and data access.
items.title: A monthly 1° global ocean mixed layer depth dataset for 1982–2023 developed with SJTU-ViT

items.summary: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.
items.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing

items.summary: Example data to reproduce the BAGFOOT2 protocol and vignette: mouse liver ATAC-seq, Fed vs Fasted (3 replicates per condition, mm10). BAGFOOT2 predicts which transcription factors change their activity between two conditions from ATAC-seq data, by combining Tn5 bias-corrected footprint depth and flanking accessibility over archetype motif clusters, with a robust Mahalanobis distance (MCD) test. Files bam_merged.tar.gz: one merged, sorted and indexed BAM file per condition (fed, fasted) bam_replicates.tar.gz: one BAM file per replicate (fed_1-3, fasted_1-3), used for HOMER (large file) tag_directories.tar.gz: HOMER tag directories of the replicates (TD_fed_1 ... TD_fasted_3) macs2.tar.gz: MACS2 peak calls (narrowPeak) per condition bg_files_fed_fasted.tar.gz: BAGFOOT2 (v2.0.0) output for Fed vs Fasted (bagplot, D2 and FDR barplots, result table) The motif database files (mm10, hg38) are NOT in this record. They are downloaded automatically by BAGFOOT2 on first use, from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20782782 How to reproduce Install BAGFOOT2: conda create -n bagfoot2 -c goldsteinlab-tech -c conda-forge -c bioconda bagfoot2 Extract the archives into one project folder: fed_fasted/bam_merged/ (merged BAM files, replicate BAM files and tag directories) fed_fasted/macs2/ (peak files) Run: bagfoot2 -b fed_fasted/bam_merged/ -p fed_fasted/macs2/ -o bg_files_fed_fasted/ -c fed -t fasted -g mm10 --bam_suffix ".sorted.bam" --cores 4 Add --homer TRUE --homer_bin /path/to/homer/bin --reps_control 1,2,3 --reps_treatment 1,2,3 to include HOMER motif enrichment. Code: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 Documentation: https://goldsteinlab-tech.github.io/BAGFOOT2/ RELATED WORKS Is supplement to: https://github.com/goldsteinlab-tech/BAGFOOT2 (Software) References: 10.5281/zenodo.20782782 (Dataset, motif database)
items.title: Supplementary Data for: BAGFOOT2 – differential transcription factor footprinting from ATAC-seq (protocol)

items.summary: We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-α}$, where $α=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Trained models forget fast ($α\approx0.55$--$0.7$), untrained ones slowly ($α\approx0.2$--$0.5$). We prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for a prompt of length $P$ and depth $L$. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits, under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} --- continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt --- can only add logarithmic factors. This is what we call the \emph{conditional no-hair theorem}: given the text generated so far, the prompt's influence on the next token vanishes as $t$ grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards $1$ seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias stops the decay early in training and reverses it after, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show it is also sufficient.
items.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
